beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB/MongoDB connection URI from an environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and never commit credentials or the full URI to source control or logs; provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.

Reuse a single long-lived MongoClient (connection pool) per process instead of creating a new client per request; configure sensible pool size and timeouts (e.g., maxPoolSize, minPoolSize, serverSelectionTimeoutMS).
Enable TLS/SSL for connections and verify server certificates; prefer private endpoints or VNet integrations rather than exposing the database endpoint publicly.
Store secrets (DB credentials, API keys) in a secrets store (Azure Key Vault) for production and read them at runtime, falling back to environment variables for local development.

Create indexes on all scalar fields used in query filters and equality predicates (e.g., trial status, phase, therapeutic area) and create appropriate compound indexes for the most common filter+sort query shapes.

For queries that page through large result sets, avoid skip-heavy pagination; use range-based or cursor (seek) pagination (e.g., use a sortable indexed field like createdAt or _id) to keep queries efficient.

Store precomputed dense numeric embeddings (as an array field) with each trial document so the app can fall back to client-side nearest-neighbor ranking if server-side vector indexes/search are unavailable.

Prefer server-side vector indexes/search when supported (create an appropriate vector index like HNSW/DiskANN/IVF on the embedding field) and put a scalar filter index alongside it for hybrid filtering+vector queries.

If server-side vector indexes are not available, perform an efficient client-side ANN using an in-memory/fast index (FAISS, hnswlib) or a batched dot-product ranking of pre-normalized embeddings rather than naive linear scan calculating cosine for every document at query time.

Keep documents reasonably small and under the MongoDB document size limit (e.g., 16 MB); store large blobs (files) in object storage with a reference in the document instead of embedding large binaries.

Model eligibility criteria in a structured, queryable form (normalized fields and arrays for inclusion/exclusion items) rather than opaque text so deterministic engines can apply rules without relying on LLMs for primary eligibility decisions.
Use projection to return only the fields required by the application (e.g., candidate id, title, short synopsis, embeddings when needed) to reduce network bandwidth and RU/IO costs.

Implement idempotent write operations (use upserts with a stable key) and retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter; be careful to make retries idempotent when operations are not naturally so.

Avoid frequent multi-document transactions when possible; design data model so most operations are single-document atomic updates. If transactions are necessary, scope them narrowly and test their performance/cost.
Use schema validation (MongoDB JSON Schema validators) on the collection to enforce the expected trial document shape (required fields, types) to catch bad seed data or malformed updates early.

Provision the cluster size and storage tier according to query patterns (CPU/memory for vector indexes) and monitor utilization; when supported, use autoscaling or adjust instance tiers to keep latency and costs acceptable.

Enable and monitor slow query logs, index usage statistics and query plans (explain) during development and after deployment to find missing indexes and expensive scans; capture explain plans for representative queries.

Use least-privilege database accounts for application access; create a user with only the needed CRUD privileges on the sample_healthcare_02 database and avoid using a wide admin key for everyday app operations.
